item.title: Four compliance frameworks, one security team: Why fragmented university security raises regulatory risk
item.description:
In Part 1 of this series, we looked at the security challenges created by fragmented, campus-by-campus environments. Higher education also faces a second pressure that makes that fragmentation harder to sustain: overlapping compliance obligations across FERPA, GLBA, HIPAA, and CMMC.

Each framework brings different requirements, reporting timelines, and consequences for failure. Managing them across one institution is already complex, but across a multi-campus university system with separate tools, staff, data stores, and governance practices, it becomes much harder to establish what happened, what data was involved, and which reporting requirements apply. With universities already facing an average of 4,388 cyberattacks per organization per week, according to the figures cited in Part 1, that regulatory complexity is becoming an operational security problem as much as a compliance one.

FERPA puts universities on a 24-hour clock

The Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act has governed the privacy of student education records since 1974, but the pressure on security teams becomes much more immediate when financial aid information is involved. If a breach compromises that data, institutions must notify the Department of Education’s Federal Student Aid office within 24 hours of discovery, leaving very little time to establish the scope of an incident while the response is still underway.

A ransomware attack discovered at 9 PM on a Friday makes the challenge easier to picture. By 9 PM Saturday, the institution may need to determine whether financial aid data was involved, understand which systems and students were affected, coordinate with legal teams, and prepare regulatory notification, all while investigators are still containing the incident and establishing what else the attackers accessed. In a multi-campus environment, that gets harder when financial aid data is spread across separate systems or when the initial discovery happens well after the compromise began.

GLBA brings financial-sector obligations into higher education

Universities may not look like traditional financial institutions, but their role in student lending and financial aid brings them within the scope of the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act’s Safeguards Rule. Covered institutions are expected to maintain a written information security program addressing areas including risk assessment, access controls, encryption, multi-factor authentication, incident response, and vendor oversight.

Reporting requirements can add further pressure. If a security event affects 500 or more consumers, the draft notes that institutions must notify federal law enforcement immediately after discovering the breach. In a university environment, where shared financial aid systems may contain records belonging to thousands of students across multiple campuses, that threshold can be reached quickly.

The multi-campus structure matters here because financial aid data rarely follows neat organizational boundaries. Students transfer between campuses, shared services may centralize information, and one system may support several institutions. A breach that begins at one campus can therefore create obligations for the wider university system, making it important to understand the scope of the incident beyond the environment where it was first detected.

HIPAA reaches well beyond the university hospital

Protected health information can exist across a much wider university environment than the hospital alone. Student health centers, counseling services, physical therapy programs, and research projects involving human subjects may all create, receive, transmit, or maintain health data, sometimes through systems that have been procured and managed separately from central IT.

A mid-sized university with a health clinic, counseling center, physical therapy program, and clinical research lab, for example, could be handling significant volumes of PHI across several independently managed environments. If one of those systems is compromised, the security team needs to establish quickly whether health information was involved and how far the incident spread.

Under the requirements set out in the draft, breaches affecting 500 or more individuals must be reported to the Department of Health and Human Services within 60 days of discovery, while some incidents also trigger media notification requirements. For universities operating across several states or with online programs, the picture becomes more complicated again. Without a reliable view of where PHI resides across the institution, determining whether those reporting obligations have been triggered can itself become part of the incident response challenge.

CMMC raises the stakes for university research

CMMC creates a different kind of pressure for institutions conducting Department of Defense-funded research or handling Controlled Unclassified Information. Research computing environments are often among the most decentralized parts of a university: individual labs build their own systems, principal investigators make independent technology decisions, and networks can evolve over years without the consistency found in centrally managed administrative IT.

CMMC Level 2 requires organizations to demonstrate implementation of 110 security practices drawn from NIST 800-171. Meeting those requirements across a diverse research estate can be difficult without limiting the flexibility researchers need to conduct their work. For institutions that rely heavily on federal research funding, the consequences also extend beyond a conventional compliance penalty because failure to meet CMMC requirements can affect contract eligibility.

One incident can trigger several compliance obligations

The real operational difficulty appears when several of these frameworks apply to the same incident. A large research university may operate student financial aid systems, health services, a hospital, and DoD-funded research environments, creating the possibility that FERPA, GLBA, HIPAA, and CMMC obligations all come into play during one investigation.

Imagine ransomware is first detected on a shared administrative system. As the investigation develops, the compromised account is found to have accessed financial aid records, student health information, and a research environment containing CUI. The university now has to understand several categories of regulated data, determine which reporting thresholds have been met, coordinate with different agencies, and maintain the evidence required for each process while still responding to the attack.

That is difficult even with centralized visibility. When security data, incident records, and compliance evidence sit across different campus tools and teams, building a reliable picture of the incident takes longer and introduces more opportunities for information to be missed.

Preparing for compliance across a multi-campus system

Meeting overlapping compliance requirements depends on being able to answer a relatively small set of questions quickly: where regulated data lives, whether it was affected, how the attacker reached it, and what happened next. University systems need enough shared visibility across campuses to answer those questions without reconstructing the entire incident manually every time something happens.

That includes consistent data classification, centralized access to security and compliance evidence, and incident response processes that have already been tested against the reporting windows institutions may face. Automation can also help teams establish the scope and context of an incident more quickly, particularly where reporting deadlines are measured in hours rather than days.

The aim is to preserve the autonomy individual campuses and research environments require while giving the wider university system enough visibility and coordination to respond consistently when regulated data is involved. As the number of overlapping obligations grows, fragmented security becomes harder to separate from compliance risk.

In Part 3 of this series, we’ll look at how a consolidated security architecture can support that model across multiple campuses, from shared visibility and threat intelligence to more coordinated detection and response.

item.title: CVE-2026-97229: Critical Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in GitLab (2026)
item.description:
Overview

On October 12, 2026, GitLab published a critical patch release for CVE-2026-97229, an integer overflow or wraparound (CWE-190) in the CI/CD regular expression compiler affecting GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE). GitLab assigned the vulnerability a CVSSv3.1 score of 10.0. Under certain conditions, a remote attacker can execute arbitrary code on an affected GitLab server through a specially crafted regular expression stored in a malicious CI/CD configuration. While the vendor supplied CVSS score indicates that exploitation is fully unauthenticated, in reproducing the exploit it was noted that an attacker must have a mechanism to plant a malicious CI/CD configuration to a repository prior to triggering the vulnerability. On GitLab instances where new users can self register and create projects, this constraint is removed.

The vulnerability affects self-managed GitLab instances across all deployment types. GitLab.com is already running a patched version, and GitLab Dedicated customers do not need to take action.

As of this writing, there is no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation of CVE-2026-97229. However, Rapid7 Intelligence has independently reproduced arbitrary code execution on an unpatched, official GitLab CE image. Given the vulnerability's maximum CVSS score, network-accessible trigger, and code execution in a GitLab application worker, Rapid7 recommends upgrading affected self-managed instances on an urgent basis, outside of normal patch cycles.

Technical overview

Rapid7's testing found that an attacker must first be able to commit a malicious CI/CD configuration file .gitlab-ci.yml, and a repository path containing UTF-8 characters to a branch in a public project. For example, an ordinary account can satisfy this prerequisite by creating a public project on a self-managed GitLab instance where that functionality is permitted. 

The crafted regular expression initially compiles in a compact US-ASCII representation and passes GitLab's regular expression validation. When it is evaluated against a specially formed, valid UTF-8 repository path, Ruby's Onigmo regular expression engine recompiles it for the new encoding after those checks have completed. An integer overflow in the compiler's program-size calculation then causes invalid regular expression instructions to be generated. The resulting loss of control-flow integrity can be used to execute attacker-controlled Onigmo VM operations in the Ruby process and run an operating system command as the GitLab git user.

Rapid7 validated the complete chain against the official GitLab 19.4.1 CE Linux amd64 image with address space layout randomization enabled. The same input did not execute against the official patched 19.4.2 CE image. Further root cause and exploit-chain details will be included in a separate Rapid7 technical analysis.

Mitigation guidance

A vendor-provided patch is available to remediate CVE-2026-97229. Organizations running affected self-managed GitLab CE or EE instances should immediately upgrade to a fixed version, without waiting for a regular patch cycle:

Affected GitLab CE/EE versions

Fixed version

All versions from 19.2 before 19.2.8

19.2.8

All versions from 19.3 before 19.3.5

19.3.5

All versions from 19.4 before 19.4.2

19.4.2

GitLab.com has already been updated, and GitLab Dedicated customers do not need to take action. Until affected self-managed instances can be upgraded, restricting anonymous access to public projects and preventing untrusted users from creating or writing to public projects can reduce exposure to the exploit path demonstrated by Rapid7. These controls address only the demonstrated delivery path and do not remediate the vulnerable regular expression compiler.

For the latest mitigation guidance, please refer to GitLab's security advisory.

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-97229 with an authenticated vulnerability check expected to be available in today’s (October 13) content release.

item.title: Ivanti Connect Secure zero-day exploited in the wild (CVE-2026-104935)
item.description:
Overview

On October 13, 2026, Ivanti published a security advisory for CVE-2026-104935, a high-severity authentication bypass by spoofing (CWE-290) affecting Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS). The vulnerability has a CVSSv3.0 score of 8.6 and allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands.

Ivanti reports that exploitation in the wild has already occurred prior to disclosure, affecting a limited number of customers. This indicates that exploitation has been occurring as a zero-day vulnerability. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) confirms exploitation in the wild, and added CVE-2026-104935 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on the same day as the vendor's public disclosure. The digital forensics firm Volexity has published a detailed blog post describing the threat actor activity, which was detected in early October 2026. Volexity notes that in addition to leveraging CVE-2026-104935 as a zero-day, the threat actor also leveraged an as-yet unpatched privilege escalation vulnerability which Ivanti are planning to patch at a later date.

According to the vendor, a portion of the vulnerability was initially discovered through its product security program and patched in the July 2026 release of 25.1.3.0. Exploitation occurred while Ivanti was working to backport the fix to the remaining supported versions.

Ivanti Connect Secure is a popular enterprise VPN solution and naturally sits on the edge of a corporate environment. The product has a history of being targeted by attackers, with zero-day exploitation of other vulnerabilities occurring back in both 2024 and 2025.

Given the confirmed exploitation, the ability to execute commands without authentication, along with the history of the product, Rapid7 recommends that organizations running affected versions apply the appropriate update on an emergency basis outside of normal patching cycles.

Mitigation guidance

Vendor-supplied updates are available to remediate CVE-2026-104935. Ivanti lists the following affected and resolved versions:

Ivanti Connect Secure affected versions

Resolved versions

22.8R2.5

item.title: Patch Tuesday - October (2026)
item.description:
Microsoft is publishing 1,413 own-product vulnerabilities on October 2026 Patch Tuesday, including 1,102 vulnerabilities in Windows. Anyone who enjoyed last month’s record-setting Patch Tuesday will love the October 2026 edition, because it’s much bigger still. As Rapid7 has noted over the course of 2026, there is every reason to suppose that vulnerability volumes will continue to rise. Microsoft is aware of exploitation in the wild for just one of the vulnerabilities published today, as well as public disclosure for two others.

Windows Shell: zero-day security feature bypass

The Windows Shell is Microsoft’s term for the GUI interaction logic for the entire OS provided by explorer.exe and associated libraries and APIs, and for the second time this year, the Windows Shell is the site of an exploited-in-the-wild zero-day vulnerability. Today’s specimen is CVE-2026-96951. Once again, the immediate prize for an attacker is a Mark of the Web (MOTW) bypass. What this means is that Windows won’t provide the user with a dialog explaining that Windows protected their PC, because in this case, it didn’t. Exploitation requires that a user opens a specially crafted malicious file or visits an attacker-controlled site, so the evergreen advice about being careful what you click remains valid. Fans of vintage operating systems should note that Windows Server 2012 doesn’t receive a patch, although Server 2012 R2 does. The advisory acknowledges reporters from multiple organizations, although none from within Microsoft. The vulnerability also affected Microsoft’s Outlook.com cloud services, although Outlook.com was patched in a build dated several weeks ago.

.NET Framework: zero-day security feature bypass

Microsoft is aware of some level of public disclosure of CVE-2026-108398, a .NET Framework security feature bypass. Exploitation requires an attacker with an existing foothold to register a malicious .NET assembly for loading by a protected process, bypassing Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) enforcement. Microsoft rebranded WDAC as App Control for Business several years ago, so you may know it under its new name. The Microsoft Learn page for Application Control for Windows points out that “your organization's data is one of its most valuable assets... and threat actors want it”, and this is, of course, correct. The patch presumably removes an attacker-controlled location from the list of places .NET Framework searches for registered assemblies, which are typically contained within DLLs and executables. If any further indications were needed that vulnerability volumes are increasing industry-wide, this is only the second month that Microsoft has published vulnerabilities with six-digit CVE numbers, but these extra-large CVEs will seem unremarkable from now on.

Outlook: multiple no-interaction RCEs

The sheer volume of vulnerabilities in recent Patch Tuesday releases can easily include several examples of potentially concerning vulnerabilities, each of which might have been more remarkable in its own right back when volumes were lower. Today, Microsoft has published five separate remote code execution vulnerabilities in Outlook where the preview pane is a vector, meaning that simply scrolling past an email in the Outlook reading pane would be sufficient to trigger exploitation. Worse still, Outlook might helpfully display the preview without any user interaction at all. All five of CVE-2026-70242, CVE-2026-97749, CVE-2026-97016, CVE-2026-88156, and CVE-2026-70291 receive fixes in the same patches. No-interaction Outlook preview pane vulnerabilities can sometimes feature prominently in state-backed actor campaigns, with CVE-2023-23397 as a prominent example in this category.

Edge: security updates unclear

In September 2026, Microsoft did not appear to publish any desktop browser security advisories between the start of the month and Patch Tuesday. In October, a slightly different approach has emerged: several recent entries in the Edge security updates release notes mention new versions of Edge which incorporate the latest updates from the Chromium project, but without detailing which vulnerabilities have been fixed, stating instead, “CVE's will be added as soon as available,” and directing readers to the Security Update Guide (SUG). At the time of writing, the SUG lists a total of zero vulnerabilities addressed in Edge in the first 13 days of October, and the “CVE’s added soon” message has been up for over a week. As a result, defenders have no obvious way of knowing which recent vulnerabilities Microsoft has addressed in Edge.

Microsoft lifecycle update

In Microsoft product lifecycle news, today sees Windows 11 24H2 Home & Pro reach end of servicing, while Windows Server 2022 moves to extended support, with free critical security updates continuing but no further feature development. Also this month, the final curtain falls for Windows Server 2012 and 2012 R2 with the expiry of the third and final year of cash-for-updates Extended Security Update (ESU) program for these aging workhorses. Microsoft lists the end of ESU Year 3 on October 14, 2026, in both cases. Microsoft has a long history of providing at least some security patches for products beyond the end of support, with Server 2008 being a case in point, but the time to move past Server 2012 is now. Office 2021 also moves into retirement on October 14; this includes the Long-Term Servicing Channel, with no ESU available in that case.

Also on October 15, 2026, Exchange Server 2016 and Exchange Server 2019 finally join the “no ESU” club, after two previous six-month reprieves. Microsoft seems to really mean it this time, since any future Exchange Server CVEs released by MSRC will stop mentioning Exchange 2016 and 2019. However, Microsoft points out that a lack of warnings does not mean those unsupported versions are not vulnerable to future security issues.
